2. Online NCF stability indicator framework for adaptive control

Section draft rewritten from manuscript2 for journal submission. Readers are assumed to be familiar with Ref. [2].

The normalized coprime factor online stability indicator (NCF OSI) demonstrated by Gomaa et al. [2] was introduced to quantify the robustness of the closed-loop system as the plant changes during the experiment. The study showed that stiffness degradation of the specimen can drive the outer controller loop toward instability through a gain amplification mechanism. In this study, we extend the analytical study to experimental implementation, discuss the challenges that arise in the experiment, and propose how to address them. The proposed framework comprises two parts, an online estimator of the indicator and an adaptive controller that gets updated accordingly. The indicator is estimated during the experiment from the desired displacement calculated by the numerical substructure and the measured actuator displacement by combining three estimator branches at each frequency, each weighted by the confidence in its evidence. The first is direct identification, bid, which estimates the closed-loop frequency response of the outer controller loop, from the desired displacement u(t) to the measured actuator displacement y(t), with the H1 cross-spectral estimator [6]. The second is output-power inference, bpow, which can detect amplification of the loop at frequencies that cannot be reliably identified. This branch compares the output power measured during the experiment against the reference recorded before the excitation. The third is the prior identification of the initial state, b0, which serves as a fallback when no sufficient information is available. The adaptive controller then utilizes the estimated indicator to scale the controller output by the adaptive factor λ to keep the loop stable with an adequate margin as the specimen degrades while retaining as much tracking performance as possible. The evaluation of the framework is discussed in detail in this section.

2.1Control loop and stability margin

In the hybrid simulation block diagram shown in Figure 1, the numerical substructure computes the desired displacement d(t) from the ground acceleration and measured force fm(t). To compensate for the transfer-system lag and improve tracking, a phase-lead compensator receives d(t) to produce the reference u(t). The outer controller C(s) takes the tracking error u(t)−y(t), where y(t) is the measured actuator displacement. Its output is scaled by the adaptive factor λ∈(0,1] to produce the command v(t) sent to the plant H(s,k).

The plant comprises the transfer system and the specimen of stiffness k. The transfer system includes the inner-loop controller, servo-valve and actuator. The control–structure interaction between the actuator and specimen is also included in the transfer-system dynamics. The measured force fm(t) is fed back to the numerical substructure and closes the numerical substructure loop, while the measured displacement y(t) provides feedback to the outer controller and closes the outer controller loop.

When the specimen degrades, its stiffness decreases and the dynamics of the outer controller loop, from u(t) to y(t), change [2]. The indicator therefore evaluates this loop. With H(s,k)=Y(s)/V(s), its open-loop and closed-loop transfer functions are

L(s,λ,k)=λC(s)H(s,k),
(1)
T(s,λ,k)=Y(s)U(s)=L(s,λ,k)1+L(s,λ,k),
(2)

where U(s) and Y(s) are the Laplace transforms of u(t) and y(t). As in [2], the distance of this loop from instability is measured by the NCF margin [1]. Unlike [2], which separates the outer controller from the plant, the whole loop is lumped here into the plant P=L with unit feedback K=1. The general definition of the margin then reduces to

bNCF(λ,k)=infωδ(L(jω,λ,k)),
(3)
δ(L)=|1+L|2(1+|L|2).
(4)

The function δ is the chordal distance between L(jω) and the critical point −1. A small δ at any frequency therefore signals a loop close to instability. All branches of the estimator evaluate a capped form of this distance,

ϕ(L)=min{δ(L),12}.
(5)

Because |1+L|2−(1+|L|2)=2ReL, the distance exceeds δ(0)=1/2 only where ReL>0. Such frequencies lie far from the critical point and say nothing about the margin. The cap removes their spurious credit and bounds the reported indicator by 1/2.

2.2Short-time spectral estimation

The margin in (3) requires the loop response at each frequency. Because this response changes as the specimen degrades, it must be obtained from the measured signals while the experiment runs. The estimator analyses short windows of u and y and updates its estimate every Δt=0.125s. Each update uses the most recent Tw=0.5s of data, so consecutive windows overlap by 75%. At fs=2048Hz, each window holds N=fsTw=1024 samples, which gives a bin spacing of 2 Hz. With n indexing the update and r=0,…,N−1 the samples in the window, the Hann-windowed discrete Fourier transforms are

Xn(ωm)=∑r=0N−1w[r]xn[r]e−j2πmr/N,x∈{u,y},
(6)

where w[r]=12{1−cos[2πr/(N−1)]} and ωm=2πmfs/N. From these transforms, the instantaneous auto- and cross-spectra are

puu,n=|Un|2,pyy,n=|Yn|2,pyu,n=YnUn*
(7)

These spectra are left unnormalized because the normalization cancels in every ratio used below, and the argument ωm is omitted for brevity. A single window is too noisy to use directly. Each spectrum is therefore smoothed recursively, following the averaging of modified periodograms [3] with exponential weighting [4], and initialized by the first complete window:

p¯ab,n(ω)=(1−ηs)p¯ab,n−1(ω)+ηspab,n(ω),ab∈{uu,yy,yu}.
(8)

The analysis is limited to the 2–100 Hz band monitored by the indicator, and the bins affected by line noise are excluded:

Ω={ωm:2≤fm≤100 Hz,fm∉[58,62] Hz},fm=ωm2π,
(9)

which leaves 47 bins. Hereafter ω∈Ω, and the subscript n denotes the operating condition (λn,kn) at update n. The current stiffness kn is unknown and is not estimated.

2.3Direct identification branch

The loop response can be identified directly from the reference u and the measured response y. The averaged spectra give the H1 estimate of the closed-loop frequency response [6] and the magnitude-squared coherence

T^n(jω)=p¯yu,n(ω)p¯uu,n(ω),γn2(ω)=|p¯yu,n(ω)|2p¯uu,n(ω)p¯yy,n(ω).
(10)

This estimate is unbiased only if the output disturbance is uncorrelated with u. In hybrid simulation, this condition is not guaranteed, because u is computed from the measured force through the numerical substructure. High coherence is therefore treated as supporting evidence rather than proof of an unbiased estimate [5].

Because this estimate can be poor, each bin receives a confidence between zero and one. The confidence combines three factors. The first is command activity, detected from the window RMS urms,n=(N−1∑run[r]2)1/2:

An={1,urms,n>ηA,0,otherwise.
(11)

The threshold ηA is approximately 4.54σu,0, where σu,0 is the command-noise standard deviation measured in a quiet record. The second factor is the input leverage. Even within an active window, some bins carry little command energy, and these bins are discounted through

ℓn(ω)=prel,n(ω)prel,n(ω)+pfloor,prel,n(ω)=p¯uu,n(ω)maxν∈ℬp¯uu,n(ν),
(12)

where ℬ is the full 2–100 Hz grid. The third factor is the coherence, which completes the confidence

cn(ω)=Anγn2(ω)ℓn(ω),0≤cn(ω)≤1.
(13)

This confidence is a weighting factor, not a probability. Where it is small, the estimate is replaced by the prior identification of the initial state, scaled by the current adaptive factor. With L0(jω)=C(jω)H(jω,k0) the full-gain loop identified at the initial stiffness k0, the prior is

Lpr,n(jω)=λnL0(jω),Tpr,n(jω)=Lpr,n(jω)1+Lpr,n(jω).
(14)

Measurement and prior are blended in the closed-loop domain, where the spectral estimate is formed. The loop is then recovered by inverting (2):

T~n(jω)=cnT^n(jω)+(1−cn)Tpr,n(jω),L^n(jω)=T~n(jω)1−T~n(jω).
(15)

As a result, a well-supported measurement governs L^n, while a weakly supported one leaves it close to the prior. Applying the capped distance to both loops gives the identified and prior margin curves

bid,n(ω)=med3{ϕ(L^n(jω))},b0,n(ω)=ϕ(Lpr,n(jω)),
(16)

where med3 is a three-bin moving median over frequency that suppresses isolated spectral outliers.

2.4Output-power inference branch

Direct identification fails when the command is weak, yet a degrading specimen can still drive the loop toward instability during such periods. The measured output power offers a second source of evidence, because it reflects the loop even without strong excitation. This power is compared against a reference taken from the first three non-overlapping windows, which are assumed to represent the initial loop at full gain. The reference power and the observed ratio are

pyy,0(ω)=medianh=1,2,3|Yh(0)(ω)|2,qobs,n(ω)=p¯yy,n(ω)pyy,0(ω),
(17)

where Yh(0) is the transform of y in reference window h. To interpret this ratio, assume that y is dominated by an equivalent output disturbance and that the spectrum of this disturbance is unchanged from the reference period. The output is then shaped by the sensitivity 1/(1+L), and a candidate loop λngL0 predicts the ratio

qmod,n(ω,g)=|1+L0(jω)1+λngL0(jω)|2.
(18)

Here, the positive scalar g is an effective change in loop magnitude, not an estimate of k. It is fitted in each bin by matching the observed and predicted ratios on a logarithmic scale:

gfit,n(ω)=arg ming∈𝒢|logqobs,n(ω)−logqmod,n(ω,g)|,
(19)

where 𝒢 holds 25 logarithmically spaced values from 0.5 to 6. Because each bin is fitted independently, the curve g(ω) is an inference model rather than an identified transfer function. A single fit is noisy, and the excitation may fade after a change is detected. The fitted change is therefore retained in a logarithmic memory initialized at g¯0=1:

logg¯n(ω)=(1−ηg)logg¯n−1(ω)+ηgloggtar,n(ω).
(20)

While the command is active (An=1), the target is gtar,n=gfit,n. The memory releases a change once the loop recovers, and recovery is detected from the band-median ratio

rΩ,n=medianω∈Ωqobs,n(ω).
(21)

When rΩ,n<1, the output power has fallen below the initial reference. The memory then decays toward g¯=1, with gtar,n=1 and ηg replaced by ηr. Otherwise, g¯n is held, so a detected change remains represented while the excitation is weak. Finally, the output-power margin curve uses the same capped distance as (16):

bpow,n(ω)=med3{ϕ(λng¯n(ω)L0(jω))}.
(22)

2.5Per-frequency fusion and reported indicator

At each frequency, the three branches now provide three margin estimates, which are combined according to the evidence behind each. The output-power branch is trusted in proportion to the size of the inferred change,

dn(ω)=clip[0,1](g¯n(ω)−1gdet−1),
(23)

which rises linearly from zero at g¯n=1 to one at g¯n=gdet. Together with the confidence cn, this detection weight sets the weights of the three branches at each frequency:

wid,n=cn,wpow,n=(1−cn)dn,w0,n=(1−cn)(1−dn).
(24)

These weights are nonnegative and sum to one. Direct identification receives the share supported by the measurement. The output-power branch receives the remainder in proportion to its detection weight, and the prior receives what neither measurement supports (Table 2). The fused margin curve is therefore

βn(ω)=wid,nbid,n(ω)+wpow,nbpow,n(ω)+w0,nb0,n(ω).
(25)

Fusion is performed bin by bin, before any reduction over frequency, so margins evaluated at different frequencies are never combined. This choice also handles the idle case without special treatment. When the command is inactive, cn=0 in every bin. An unchanged loop then reads its gain-scaled prior, and a bin with a remembered change continues to report it.

To drive the adaptive controller, the fused curve is reduced to a single value. The instantaneous indicator is the second-smallest value of βn over Ω,

binst,n=βn,(2)=βn(ω*,n),
(26)

where ω*,n is the governing frequency. Discarding the lowest bin prevents a single outlier from governing the estimate, at the cost of attenuating a genuine minimum that is only one bin wide. To suppress fluctuations between updates, the reported indicator is smoothed in time,

bOSI,n=(1−ηb)bOSI,n−1+ηbbinst,n,
(27)

and the adaptive law uses it to update λn+1. Figure 2 summarizes one complete update, from the measured signals to the adaptive factor, and Table 1 lists the estimator parameters.

2.6Assumptions and limitations

The estimator relies on four assumptions, and each one limits how the reported indicator should be interpreted.

  1. The identification branch assumes that the output disturbance is uncorrelated with u. Feedback through the numerical substructure can violate this assumption and bias T^n even at high coherence [5].
  2. The output-power branch assumes that the disturbance spectrum is unchanged from the reference period and that the first 1.5 s represent the initial loop at full gain. A change in disturbance intensity or in the command-driven response can therefore alter qobs without any change in stability.
  3. The factor g is real. The output-power branch therefore captures changes in loop magnitude but not in loop phase.
  4. Band limitation, trimming, and temporal smoothing mean that bOSI is not a guaranteed lower bound on the full-frequency margin bNCF. The reported indicator also follows abrupt changes with a delay set by ηb.

References

  1. K. Glover and D. McFarlane, “Robust stabilization of normalized coprime factor plant descriptions with H∞-bounded uncertainty,” IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control, vol. 34, no. 8, pp. 821–830, 1989. doi:10.1109/9.29424
  2. M. Gomaa, E. D. Patino, J. N. Villamizar, J. W. Condori Uribe, and S. J. Dyke, “An online stability indicator for real-time hybrid simulation emphasizing physical substructure degradation,” author manuscript.
  3. P. D. Welch, “The use of fast Fourier transform for the estimation of power spectra: A method based on time averaging over short, modified periodograms,” IEEE Transactions on Audio and Electroacoustics, vol. 15, no. 2, pp. 70–73, 1967. doi:10.1109/TAU.1967.1161901
  4. S. W. Roberts, “Control chart tests based on geometric moving averages,” Technometrics, vol. 1, no. 3, pp. 239–250, 1959. doi:10.1080/00401706.1959.10489860
  5. U. Forssell and L. Ljung, “Closed-loop identification revisited,” Automatica, vol. 35, no. 7, pp. 1215–1241, 1999. doi:10.1016/S0005-1098(99)00022-9
  6. J. S. Bendat and A. G. Piersol, Random Data: Analysis and Measurement Procedures, 4th ed., Hoboken, NJ: Wiley, 2010.
